title: Carrying the head home
hook: Bhai Jaita carries the Guru's head to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah burns his own house to cremate the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chandni Chowk, where the ninth Guru gave his head but not his faith. Your line was for another's faith. Did you speak up for someone who believes differently? Day eighty.

When someone dies far from home, someone has to bring them back. Anyone who has done it knows: the paperwork, the long drive, the phone calls, the sitting with the body. It's one of the most loving and least noticed jobs there is. After the Guru was killed in Chandni Chowk, his body lay in the square under guard. Tradition says the authorities meant it as a warning, and that nobody dared go near it. The Sikhs in Delhi were watched and afraid. And yet two men, on the same night, decided the Guru would not be left there. Today, the brave, quiet work of bringing him home.
screen: `SOMEONE HAS TO BRING THEM BACK.` → `THE BODY IN THE SQUARE.` → `TWO MEN, ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The first was Bhai Jaita, a Sikh from a community that society treated as low caste. Tradition says that in the confusion of a dust storm that night, he slipped through, took up the Guru's head, wrapped it, and set off for Anandpur, hundreds of miles away, traveling in secret, mostly at night. When he arrived, the young Gobind Rai, now the tenth Guru at nine years old, received his father's head. Tradition says he embraced Jaita and spoke a line Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas, Jaita's own community, are the Guru's own sons. A boy honoring a man the world looked down on, calling him family. Jaita later took initiation and became Bhai Jiwan Singh. The second man was Lakhi Shah, a wealthy trader who carried goods by bullock cart. In the same storm, tradition says, he and his sons hid the Guru's body in a cart under a load of cotton, and drove it to their house outside the city. They couldn't hold a public cremation; soldiers would have come. So Lakhi Shah built a pyre inside his own home, laid the Guru's body in it, and set his house on fire. To the neighbors, it looked like an accident. It was his home, given as a funeral. Today Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands there, near the Parliament of India. Two men. One carried the head to a nine-year-old son. One burned down everything he had. Neither was a Guru, and both brought him home. With them, the story of the ninth Guru ends.
screen: `BHAI JAITA TAKES THE HEAD.` · `RANGRETE GURU KE BETE.` · `LAKHI SHAH'S CART OF COTTON.` · `A HOUSE GIVEN AS A FUNERAL.` · then, large: `BRING HIM HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a brave, quiet kindness, starting with choosing one. Settle and breathe. Think of a loving task that nobody wants to do and nobody will thank you for. Visiting someone difficult. Sorting a relative's things. Sitting with someone in a hospital. Calling the family nobody calls. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without being seen, like a man walking through a dust storm. Let it feel possible. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Jaita. The Sikh who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head from Delhi to Anandpur, whom the young Guru called a son of the Guru.
Your line: bring him home. Today, do the loving task you thought of, or one step of it, and tell no one. Day eighty.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Jaita and Lakhi Shah Vanjara at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Anandpur Sahib, where the head was cremated, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj in Delhi, where the body was.

fork.setup: you're Lakhi Shah. you have the Guru's body hidden in your cart, and a public cremation would bring soldiers. what do you do?
options: leave it at the city gate.
build a pyre in your own house and burn it down.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the Rangretas are the Guru's own sons, the tenth Guru's words to Bhai Jaita.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone rescued a body.
what it means: two men risked everything to bring the Guru home, and a boy Guru called the one the world looked down on family.
what a scholar hears: the head was cremated at Anandpur (Gurdwara Sis Ganj there) and the body at Raisina (Rakab Ganj); Jaita became Bhai Jiwan Singh.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Bhai Jaita (Jiwan Singh) and Lakhi Shah Vanjara, November 1675
